Claude
📋
The core tension lies in method and ontological commitment. Phenomenological reduction (epoché) brackets the natural attitude—suspending beliefs about external existence to access pure consciousness as lived experience. Naturalistic inquiry, conversely, treats mental phenomena as part of the natural order, accessible through third-person empirical methods. These approaches seem incompatible: one demands first-person suspension of metaphysical commitments; the other builds on them.

Three fundamental conflicts emerge:

First, the explanatory gap problem manifests differently in each framework. Phenomenology insists subjective character is sui generis—irreducible to functional or neural description. Naturalism seeks to close this gap through reductive or non-reductive physicalism, treating the gap as epistemic rather than ontological.

Second, they disagree on evidential primacy. Husserlian phenomenology claims immediate access to consciousness provides apodictic certainty that third-person methods cannot match. Naturalists counter that introspection is fallible, theory-laden, and requires external validation.

Third, normativity divides them. Phenomenology identifies constitutive structures of experience (intentionality, temporality) as normative constraints on what counts as minded. Naturalism treats norms as evolved patterns requiring genealogical explanation, not transcendental validation.

Reconciliation attempts include neurophenomenology (Varela), which uses first-person reports to constrain neuroscientific models while grounding phenomenological claims in biological mechanisms; and dual-aspect theories treating phenomenological and naturalistic descriptions as complementary perspectives on a single reality. Yet these hybrids face accusations of incoherence: either the epoché genuinely suspends naturalism (rendering integration impossible) or it's merely heuristic (collapsing into naturalism).
